title: Environmental racism

definition.text: The disproportionate burden of environmental hazards, pollution and ecological damage on marginalized communities and people of colour.

facts.text: It is built into policy-making at home and abroad and is a form of structural racism that creates health hierarchies.
Benjamin Chavis coined the term in 1982 while opposing a PCB waste landfill in Warren County, North Carolina.
Its causes include competition for cheap land, dismissive attitudes to harmful projects, and affected communities' lack of political power, mobility and money.
Some critics argue cost–benefit analysis can feed it by valuing environmental resources by their usefulness to society, through willingness to pay.
Communities of colour and low-income communities bear more of the air and water pollution from fossil fuel processing; such places are called sacrifice zones.
Between 1989 and 1994 an estimated 2,611 metric tons of hazardous waste went from OECD countries to non-OECD countries.
A US Government Accountability Office study after the 1982 Warren County protests was among the first to link the race and income of communities to hazardous waste sites.

definition.text: Payments or investments made to people judged to be harmed by the presence of industry.

facts.text: Possible recipients include people living near industry, disaster victims and climate refugees.
They can range from direct payouts to funds for cleaning waste sites, air monitors in low-income neighbourhoods, or public transport.

definition.text: A legal theory that ecosystems and species hold inherent rights, much as humans hold fundamental human rights.

facts.text: It rejects treating nature as a 'resource' to own, use and degrade, as most twentieth-century laws did.
Two arguments support it: rights that flow from human existence should also flow from nature's existence, and human survival depends on healthy ecosystems.
Proponents say ordinary environmental laws are subordinate to economic interests and only partly slow damage driven by the economy.
For example, the US Endangered Species Act only acts once a species is heading toward extinction.
Ecuador amended its constitution in 2008 to recognise nature's rights, drawing on respect for Pachamama; Bolivia followed with its own provisions.
The 2010 Universal Declaration of the Rights of Mother Earth was adopted in Bolivia by representatives of 130 nations.
As of May 2024, close to 500 rights of nature laws existed in 40 countries, from local to national level.
Law professor Christopher Stone argued for giving natural entities legal standing, with guardians able to sue on their behalf.
